newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania programme seeks stability, growth by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Romania programme seeks stability, growth by 2000.

text.p: Romania's reformist government submitted to parliament on Wednesday a programme to stabilise the economy and achieve growth by the year 2000 as a step towards securing membership of NATO and the European Union.

The 120-page programme, presented by Prime Minister designate Victor Ciorbea, was likely to secure approval from the governing coalition which threw leftists out of office in last month's general election.
The programme contains no specific targets for growth, inflation or the budget deficit.
Ciorbea described the document as a "political programme" intended as a first step towards the market after seven years of government by ex-communists.
The programme's main points include:

-- Achieving economic recovery and moving towards long-term economic development by modifying the role of the state in allotting national resources, creating an integrated market system and developing competition.
-- Reducing poverty and consolidating the middle class as the most important guarantor of democracy and stability.
-- Speeding up privatisation and restructuring of industry, making the process more open and preventing abuses and conflict of interest.

-- Opening the economy, attracting foreign investment by eliminating bureaucratic barriers and corruption, acknowledging the right of foreign investors to acquire land needed to complete investment projects.
-- Eliminating restrictions on repatriation of earnings and drawing a distinction between direct and portfolio investment.
-- Liberalising foreign exchange markets and expanding capital markets.
-- Controlling the budget deficit through tougher financial discipline and halting credits and subsidies to chronically loss-making state companies.
-- Encouraging the private sector by cutting taxes on profits and on agriculture and introducing a comprehensive income tax system. Improving tax collection and cracking down on evasion.
-- Liberalising imports and actively promoting exports.
-- Improving communications and transport, promoting the growth of tourism.
-- Pursuing cautious monetary policy and halting finance for agriculture through central bank "special credits".
-- Consolidating private property in agriculture, completing land reform launched in 1991.
-- Cutting unemployment to 5.0 percent from present nominal rates of more than six percent by the year 2000.
-- Raising child and unemployment benefit and pensions.
-- Stimulating housing construction.
